item.title: Early Post-ROSC Laboratory Phenotypes and Clinical Outcomes after Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest: A 10-Year National Cohort Study
item.description:
Background: Prior phenotyping in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) relied predominantly on prehospital indicators, which neither describe nor grade the underlying ischemia-reperfusion injury. We aimed to derive laboratory-based phenotypes and describe their clinical characteristics and outcome associations.

Methods: We conducted a retrospective cohort study of adult resuscitated OHCA patients of presumed cardiac etiology between 01/02/2011 and 01/01/2022, linking Singapore's national OHCA and cardiovascular databases. Unsupervised latent class analysis (LCA) was applied to 14 laboratory variables within six hours post-return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC). Stability was confirmed through split-sample validation. Logistic regression and Cox proportional hazards model, adjusted for age, sex and initial cardiac rhythm, assessed poor neurological recovery at hospital discharge, 30-day and 3-year mortality.

Results: Among 1514 eligible patients (median age 65.0 years, 73.6% males), LCA identified three distinct phenotypes: multi-organ dysfunction (MOD, N=286), homeostatic (HOM, N=967), and immune-dysregulated (IMD, N=261), independently reproduced in derivation (entropy=0.817) and replication (entropy=0.892) subsamples. The most discriminative variables were creatinine, eosinophil and lymphocyte. Compared to MOD, both HOM (aOR: 0.50, 95% CI 0.30-0.78, p=0.004) and IMD (aOR: 0.46, 95% CI 0.26-0.78, p=0.005) phenotypes had significantly lower odds of poor neurological recovery. This pattern was consistent for 30-day mortality (HOM aHR: 0.71, 95% CI 0.61-0.83; IMD aHR: 0.78, 95% CI 0.64-0.94) and 3-year mortality (HOM aHR: 0.70, 95% CI 0.60-0.82; IMD aHR: 0.74, 95% CI 0.62-0.90), all p≤0.01.

Conclusion: Early post-ROSC laboratory data identified three prognostically distinct phenotypes among resuscitated OHCA patients. These exploratory findings support external validation and investigation of phenotype-guided therapies.

item.title: The Epidemiology of Paediatric Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest in Australia and New Zealand: A Report from The Australasian Resuscitation Outcomes Consortium Epistry (Aus-ROC)
item.description:
Background: This first epidemiological study of paediatric out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (pOHCA) across Australia and New Zealand explores the incidence, patient and event characteristics, both overall and by developmental age groups, and examines factors associated with outcomes.

Methods: All pOHCAs (aged <18 years) attended by emergency medical services (EMS) in Australia and New Zealand from 2017 to 2023 were included. Crude incidence rates (per 100,000 person-years) were calculated for EMS-attended and EMS-treated cases. Logistic regression models were used to identify associations between patient and arrest characteristics and survival (event and 30-day/hospital discharge).

Results: EMS attended 4,779 cases and treated 3,139 (65.7%). Incidence rates for EMS-attended and EMS-treated cases were 10.1 and 6.6, respectively; with a bimodal age distribution peaking in infants (65.4) and adolescents (11.4). Most EMS-attended cases were unwitnessed (66.9%), of medical origin (60.1%), had initial non-shockable rhythms (91.1%), occurred in private residences (74.3%), and received bystander cardiopulmonary resuscitation (62.7%). Few (1.6%) received bystander defibrillation. Arrest characteristics varied widely between age groups. Survival to 30-days/hospital discharge in EMS-treated cases was 10.0% (highest in late childhood [15.4%] and lowest in infants [7.9%]). Multivariable analysis identified that increasing age was positively associated with event survival, whilst bystander-witnessed arrest, initial shockable rhythm, arrest aetiology, and EMS response time were significant predictors of short and long-term survival.

Conclusion: The incidence, patient characteristics, and survival outcomes of pOHCA in our region differ significantly by age groups. Age- and context-specific prevention and resuscitation strategies are essential for reducing the burden and improving survival outcomes.

item.title: Opioid-Associated vs Undifferentiated Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest: Examining differences in outcomes and the relationship with Utstein variables
item.description:
Background: The pathophysiology of out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) due to opioid toxicity is different from other OHCAs. Our aims were to determine: (1) whether opioid-toxicity is associated with OHCA outcomes; and, (2) whether the relationship between Utstein variables and outcomes differ between those with opioid-associated (OA) and other OHCA.

Methods: We analysed adult emergency medical services (EMS)-treated OHCAs from the British Columbia Cardiac Arrest Registry. Using post-mortem toxicological investigations, death certificates, and hospital-based diagnoses, we classified as OA-OHCA or "undifferentiated OHCA". We fit a multivariable logistic regression model to assess the association between OA-OHCA (versus undifferentiated OHCA) and favourable neurological outcome at hospital discharge. We then added pre-specified interaction terms to individual models for: sex, initial cardiac rhythm, bystander CPR, witnessed arrest, and location type.

Results: Of 10,786 OHCAs: 1349 (13%) were OA-OHCA, of whom 331 (25%) were female, and the median age was 40 years (IQR 31-50); 9437 (87%) were undifferentiated, of whom 2910 (31%) were female, and the median age was 70 years (IQR 58-81). We did not detect an association between OA-OHCA (OR 1.02, 95% CI 0.77, 1.35) and survival with favourable neurological outcomes. Models adding interaction terms demonstrated statistically significant interactions for: sex (p=0.032), initial cardiac rhythm (p=0.024), and bystander-witnessed status (p=<0.001).

Conclusion: Overall, we did not detect an association between opioid toxicity and outcomes. In models with interaction terms, the relationship between Utstein and outcomes differed between opioid-associated and other OHCAs, highlighting the impact opioid-associated cases may have in observational OHCA analyses.

item.title: Outcomes Following Impedance Threshold Device Use During Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest
item.description:
Background: Existing work is equivocal regarding the benefit of impedance threshold device (ITD) use among patients experiencing out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA). We examined the association of ITD use with prehospital outcomes and longer-term dispositions in a nationally representative sample of OHCA patients.

Methods: We included adult, non-traumatic, OHCA scene runs from the 2024 ESO Data Collaborative. We compared patients treated with (a) ITD only; (b) ITD and active compression-decompression device (ITD+ACD); and (c) neither device (no ITD). Prehospital outcomes included return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) and survival to hospital arrival (SHA); disposition outcomes included survival to hospital discharge and favorable neurologic outcome (i.e., discharge to home). We used multivariate logistic regression to examine the association of treatment group with outcomes, adjusting for demographics and several potential confounders.

Results: We included 97,439 patient records (85.3% no ITD; 13.1% ITD only; 1.6% ITD+ACD). Disposition outcomes were available for 13,026 patients (23.3%). ROSC was higher for patients treated with ITD only (26.7%) than those treated with no ITD (23.8%; aOR=1.09 [1.04, 1.14]); a similar pattern emerged for SHA. Conversely, survival to discharge was lower for patients treated with ITD only (23.9%) than those treated with no ITD (32.0%; aOR=0.68, [.61, .76]); a similar pattern emerged for favorable neurologic outcome. The ITD+ACD group showed more extreme versions of the trends observed for ITD only.

Conclusions: ITD use was associated with improved prehospital outcomes but worsened dispositional outcomes among patients experiencing OHCA, suggesting this device may prove beneficial early in resuscitation of OHCA patients.

item.title: Spectral Characteristics and Parameters of Pulse Oximetry Waveforms for Assessing Resuscitation Status
item.description:
Background: Real-time assessment of physiological resuscitation status is critical for guiding personalised cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) and avoiding unnecessary harm from prolonged chest compressions. Non-invasive, objectively trackable tools for this purpose remain limited.

Methods: This multicentre retrospective study (2013-2018) included 451 adult patients with cardiac arrest (497 CPR episodes) from 14 Chinese tertiary hospitals, comprising 158 Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest (OHCA) episodes with prehospital SpO2/ECG monitoring continued upon ED arrival and full pulse oximetry plethysmography (POP)/ECG/end-tidal carbon dioxide (ETCO2) monitoring established in the ED, and 339 In-Hospital Cardiac Arrest (IHCA) episodes occurring in the ED. We analysed POP waveforms across four statuses: compression-only (CC), chest compression with return of spontaneous circulation (CC+ROSC, spontaneous circulation during ongoing compressions), non-compression without ROSC, and spontaneous circulation-only (SC). Time-domain (area under the POP curve [POPAUC]) and frequency-domain spectral features were evaluated against clinically documented ROSC.

Results: A frequency-domain "hybrid" pattern during the CC+ROSC identified ROSC with 100% specificity (PPV 1.000). In CC status,POPAUC was higher in stable-ROSC than unstable-ROSC (3232.2±1008.2 vs. 2769.6±1013.0 PVPG, P=0.007). The POPAUC was lower in CC+ROSC status than in SC status for stable-ROSC (2768.2±997.8 vs. 3335.8±842.4 PVPG, P=0.001), but the reverse was observed for unstable-ROSC (2697.5±941.0 vs. 1338.1±952.6 PVPG, P<0.001). POP waveforms disappearance with concurrent ECG presence identified pulseless electrical activity with 100% specificity.

Conclusion: Pulse oximetry plethysmography waveform analysis-using signals already available on standard monitors-may provide a non-invasive, real-time approach that may help identify ROSC during ongoing compressions and distinguish between stable and unstable circulation.

item.title: Amiodarone After Conversion From a Non-shockable to a Shockable Rhythm in Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest A Propensity Score-Matched Analysis from the German Resuscitation Registry
item.description:
Background: Amiodarone should be administered after three shocks according the current ERC ALS guidelines. However, its effect in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) patients with an initial non-shockable rhythm who subsequently convert to a shockable rhythm is not established.

Methods: We performed a retrospective observational cohort study using data from the German Resuscitation Registry. Adult patients with non-traumatic OHCA, having an initial non-shockable rhythm and subsequently received at least two defibrillations were included. Propensity-score-matched patient pairs (1:1) were analysed to compare outcomes between patients who received amiodarone during resuscitation and those who did not. The primary outcome was survival to hospital discharge. Secondary outcomes included hospital admission with return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC), 24-hour survival, survival to hospital discharge, and favourable neurological outcome at hospital discharge.

Results: Of 5,535 patients included 3,181 received amiodarone and 2,354 did not. After propensity-score matching, 1,843 patients remained in each group. Amiodarone administration was associated with higher rates of hospital admission with ROSC (26.7% vs. 23.0%; OR 1.22, 95% confidence interval 1.05-1.42), 24-hour survival (21.4% vs. 14.7%; OR 1.58, 95% CI 1.33-1.87), and survival to hospital discharge (6.5% vs. 4.2%; OR 1.58, 95% CI 1.18-2.12). Favourable neurological outcome at hospital discharge was not statistically significant (3.7% vs. 2.9%; OR 1.31, 95% CI 0.91-1.89).

Conclusions: In OHCA patients with an initial non-shockable rhythm who subsequently converted to a shockable rhythm, amiodarone administration was associated with improved short-term and long-term survival, but not with a statistically significant improved favourable neurological outcome. Future controlled studies might define the proper (earlier) time of amiodarone administration.

item.title: Impact of Cardiac Rhythm Dynamics during Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation on Clinical Outcomes in Patients Treated with Extracorporeal Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation (ECPR): A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
item.description:
Background: Although the initial presenting cardiac rhythm is an established prognostic factor for extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation, heart rhythm dynamics during conventional cardiopulmonary resuscitation remain poorly studied. We evaluated how the evolution of rhythm affects neurological outcomes and survival among recipients of extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation.

Methods: We systematically searched PubMed and Embase for studies evaluating rhythm dynamics, focusing on Rhythm Improvement (from non-shockable to shockable) or Rhythm Decay (from shockable to non-shockable). The primary outcome was survival with a favorable neurological outcome at the longest follow-up; the secondary outcome was overall survival. A random-effects model analysis with the Hartung-Knapp adjustment was used.

Results: Ten observational studies evaluating 5183 subjects with out-of-hospital cardiac arrest treated with extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation were included. Rhythm improvement was associated with a higher probability of a favorable neurological outcome (RR 3.12, 95% CI 1.26-7.74; GRADE: Low) compared with refractory non-shockable rhythms. Conversely, rhythm decay reduced the likelihood of a favorable neurological outcome compared with a sustained shockable rhythm (RR 0.41, 95% CI 0.21-0.80; GRADE: Moderate). Notably, decay toward asystole showed a robust negative association with good neurological recovery (RR 0.20, 95% CI 0.09-0.45; GRADE: Moderate), whereas decay toward pulseless electrical activity did not reach statistical significance (RR 0.62, 95% CI 0.31-1.25; GRADE: Low).

Conclusions: Rhythm dynamics provide valuable prognostic insights for candidates for extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation. Rhythm decay toward asystole may predict resuscitation failure and poor neurological survival, suggesting that it should prompt a critical re-evaluation of the appropriateness of extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation.

item.title: Non-enrolment and non-completion of cardiac rehabilitation among survivors of out-of-hospital cardiac arrest with ischaemic aetiology: a nationwide register-based cohort study
item.description:
Background: Survival after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) of ischaemic aetiology is increasing, yet access to and completion of cardiac rehabilitation remain uncertain.

Aim: To investigate non-enrolment in and non-completion of cardiac rehabilitation among OHCA survivors of ischaemic aetiology including temporal trends, and to examine sociodemographic characteristics associated with non-participation and non-completion.

Methods: This nationwide Danish register-based cohort study included adults surviving ≥30 days after a first-time OHCA between 2019 and 2023. Multivariable logistic regression models were used to examine the association between non- enrolment and non-completion, respectively, and sociodemographic parameters of age, sex, cohabitation, comorbidity, education, and employment.

Results: A total of 1,684 OHCA survivors were included. Overall, 55% did not enrol in CR, and among those who enrolled, 50% did not complete the programme. Non-enrolment was highest in 2020-2022 (60-62%) and declined to 43% in 2023. Survivors who were retired had higher odds of non-enrolment (OR 1.74, 95% CI 1.42-2.44), whereas higher education (OR 0.76, 95% CI 0.55-0.98) and moderate/severe comorbidity (OR 0.53, 95% CI 0.43-0.65) were associated with lower odds of non-enrolment. No sociodemographic characteristics were significantly associated with non-completion.

Conclusion: A large proportion of OHCA survivors of ischaemic aetiology either did not enrol in or did not complete cardiac rehabilitation. The findings underscore the need for systematic referral to cardiac rehabilitation after OHCA and more tailored rehabilitation approaches.

item.title: Most Older Long-Term Care Residents in Oslo Have Documented Do-Not-Resuscitate Status: A Cross-Sectional Study
item.description:
With population aging, understanding the frequency and distribution of decisions to attempt or withhold cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) in long-term care populations is increasingly important. In Oslo, CPR status, that is, an advance decision about whether CPR should or should not be attempted, is systematically assessed and documented for all long-term care residents. Comprehensive register data therefore provide a unique opportunity to assess advance CPR decisions at the population level. We obtained cross-sectional data on the documented CPR status of nearly all persons aged 50+ years admitted to public or private long-term care facilities in Oslo between 2018 and 2023 (N=7,860). We examined the proportion of long-term care residents with documented positive CPR status (CPR should be attempted) and used multivariable logistic regression to analyze the associations between documented positive CPR status and age, sex, marital status, primary contact (e.g., son, daughter, spouse, professional), functional limitations, institutional relocations, duration of stay, and year of admission. We found that 9.2% of long-term care residents had documented positive CPR status. Documented positive CPR status was related to younger age, fewer limitations, shorter duration of stay, and fewer relocations. Compared with residents first admitted in 2018, documented positive CPR status was less likely among those first admitted between 2019 and 2022, but not among those first admitted in 2023. There was no evidence that documented positive CPR status was related to sex, marital status, primary contact. Our findings provide population-level evidence on documented CPR status in long-term care and highlight the need for future research on how such decisions are made.

item.title: Time to Return of Spontaneous Circulation and Long-Term Outcomes in Bystander-Witnessed Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest Survivors
item.description:
Background and aims: Immediate Out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) survival is time-sensitive, however, evidence linking resuscitation time to recovery is limited. We examined time from emergency call to return of spontaneous circulation (time-to- ROSC) and survivor outcomes.

Methods: From the Danish Cardiac Arrest Registry, we included adults with bystander-witnessed OHCA (2016-2023) surviving ≥30 days, without prior anoxic brain damage or nursing home admission. Time-to-event and multivariable regression analyses stratified by time-to-ROSC (A:0-10, B:11-18, C:>18 minutes) assessed 11- month anoxic brain damage and nursing home admission, plus long-term survival and return-to-work through December 2024.

Results: We included 2,583 patients (n=875, 869, 839; groups A-C, respectively), 78% male; median age 65; median time-to-ROSC 14 min. Anoxic brain damage increased with time-to-ROSC (A-C: 0.3%, 1.8%, 3.2%; p<0.001). Adjusted analyses showed an overall association (p=0.03); HRs: 5.58 (95% CI 1.58-19.64) for B and 9.98 (95% CI 2.93-33.96) for C versus A. Nursing home admission decreased with time-to- ROSC (A-C: 3.1%, 2.2%, 1.3%; p=0.04), but adjustments attenuated the association (p=0.3). Long-term survival was similar (5-year Kaplan-Meier estimate: 79%; 95% CI 77-81%; p = 0.80; adjusted p = 0.99). Among employed patients (n=177, 168, 179), return-to-work was similar (5-year cumulative incidence: 60%; 95% CI 56-65%; p = 0.31; adjusted p = 0.29).

Conclusions: In bystander-witnessed 30-day OHCA survivors, prolonged resuscitation does not preclude recovery, time-to-ROSC was associated with anoxic brain damage but not nursing home admission, return-to-work, or long-term survival.

item.title: Automated External Defibrillators for In-Hospital Cardiac Arrest: A Systematic Review
item.description:
Background: Automated external defibrillators (AEDs) improve survival after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest, but their role in in-hospital cardiac arrest (IHCA) remains uncertain. This systematic review evaluates whether ward-accessible AED capability prior to code blue team arrival improves survival and neurologic outcomes compared with standard resuscitation systems.

Methods: Six databases were searched. Eligible studies compared AED use to manual defibrillation in IHCA outside specialized areas. Primary outcome was survival with favorable neurological status (CPC 1-2, mRS 0-3, or no deterioration from baseline). Secondary outcomes included ROSC, survival at 24 hours, survival to discharge, 30-day survival, CPR quality, and timing metrics. Three independent reviewers performed study selection, data extraction, and risk-of-bias assessment. Due to substantial heterogeneity, results were synthesized descriptively.

Results: Six reports from five unique study cohorts met inclusion criteria (total screened = 5,510). Neurologically favorable survival was inconsistent. One study reported improved outcomes following a combined AED-and-training intervention, whereas the largest multicentre cohort found no significant difference in neurological disability among survivors (adjusted relative risk 1.01, 95% CI 0.93-1.09). ROSC and survival to discharge were not consistently improved. Only one study directly quantified AED-associated compression pauses, and effects on time to defibrillation varied by setting.

Conclusion: Available evidence is insufficient to determine whether routine ward-level AED deployment improves IHCA outcomes. Included studies were observational and heterogeneous and CPR quality and training were incompletely characterized. Potential benefit from earlier defibrillation in shockable rhythms must be weighed against possible compression interruptions. Contemporary comparative studies are needed.

item.title: Prehospital Prognostication after Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest in Tertiary Care Centers: The R-EDByUS Score in the JAAM-OHCA Registry
item.description:
Aim: The R-EDByUS score predicts unfavorable neurological outcomes after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) using prehospital variables alone, with separate models based on return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) status at hospital arrival. However, whether the score remains valid in patients transported to tertiary care centers is uncertain. We therefore aimed to validate it externally in this setting.

Methods: Using the JAAM-OHCA Registry, we analyzed adult patients with presumed cardiogenic OHCA transported to tertiary care centers. The regression-based R-EDByUS score was applied to predict unfavorable neurological outcome (Cerebral Performance Category 3-5) at 1 month in the prehospital ROSC and ongoing cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) cohorts. Discrimination and calibration were assessed, and score performance was examined across in-hospital intervention subgroups (percutaneous coronary intervention, targeted temperature management, and extracorporeal membrane oxygenation). We also assessed the proportion of patients with unfavorable outcomes among those with a predicted probability ≥99%.

Results: Of 29,345 patients, 3,305 were classified into the prehospital ROSC cohort and 26,040 into the ongoing CPR cohort. The score showed good discrimination, with areas under the curve of 0.906 and 0.913, and good calibration in the prehospital ROSC cohort. Discrimination was lower among patients who received PCI, TTM, or ECMO in the ongoing CPR cohort. Among patients with a predicted probability ≥99%, 100% (112/112; prehospital ROSC) and 99.9% (20,560/20,588; ongoing CPR) had unfavorable outcomes.

Conclusion: The R-EDByUS score showed good discrimination in the JAAM-OHCA Registry, supporting its use for early risk stratification in cardiogenic OHCA even in tertiary care centers.
